title: Four ways to water a garden
word: Four ways to water a garden
hook: Teresa: prayer can be like carrying buckets, a water wheel, a stream, or rain

segments.voice: Yesterday, Carmel, and Elijah on Horeb, where God wasn't in the wind or the fire. Your line was the still small voice. Did you find a minute with everything turned off? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-four.

A Carmelite nun in Spain is asked by her confessors to write down how she prays. Her name is Teresa, from the city of Ávila. She isn't a trained theologian, and she says so. So instead of a system, she reaches for a garden. Someone is handed a patch of hard, weedy ground and told to make it grow. In her account, the Lord has already pulled up the weeds and put in good plants. The job left is water. And there are, she says, four ways to get it there. Today's word is her picture: four ways to water a garden.

First way: you draw water from a well by hand and carry it in buckets. Heavy, slow, and some days the well seems dry. Teresa says this is how prayer often begins: effort, attention, gathering a wandering mind, again and again. Second way: a water wheel, the kind turned by a crank, lifting many buckets at once. Less sweat, more water. Prayer here grows quieter; the soul rests a little, and something is given that you didn't haul up yourself. Third way: a stream or a river running through the garden. Now the gardener mostly just guides where the water goes. Fourth way: rain. The gardener does nothing at all. The sky does it. Notice the shape. As the ways go on, the gardener works less and the Lord gives more. Teresa doesn't call the buckets a failure. They're where she says people begin, and she's frank that she spent long, dry years there herself. She also doesn't promise the steps come in a neat line. The garden can go back to buckets. Psalm sixty-five has a line that fits her fourth way: "Thou visitest the earth, and waterest it." And Paul puts the whole thing in one sentence about his own work: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase." Look back over this week and it's been a week of letting go. Francis and Lady Poverty, perfect joy in the cold, brother sun and sister water, an instrument of peace, a life that preaches, Elijah in the hush. Teresa adds her own: you keep carrying the bucket, and you leave the rain to God.
screen: `THE GARDENER WORKS LESS, GOD GIVES MORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name how your prayer, or your inner life, feels right now. Sit and breathe, and ask honestly which picture fits. Buckets: work, and not much coming up. A wheel: some rhythm, a little easier. A stream: things moving on their own. Rain: something given you didn't earn. There's no right answer, and no grade. Just name it. If you pray, you can tell God which one it is today. If you don't, just notice the dry places and the wet ones. The bell holds the time.
Four ways to water a garden. Teresa of Ávila's picture of prayer: buckets, a wheel, a stream, and rain, with less of our work and more of God's as it goes.
screen: `FOUR WAYS TO WATER A GARDEN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: sometimes buckets, sometimes rain. Today, if something feels like hauling water, keep hauling, and don't take it as proof you're doing it wrong. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Teresa's image of the four waters is taught in Carmelite houses and retreats as a way to describe the growth of prayer, from effortful meditation toward quieter prayer received as gift.

notes: The four waters are paraphrased from Teresa's Life (usually chs. 11–21); confirm chapter range and that the four are well, water wheel (noria), stream/river, and rain.
Hook: 'asked by her confessors to write down how she prays' and 'she isn't a trained theologian, and she says so' paraphrase Teresa's own framing in the Life; confirm.
'She spent long, dry years there herself' paraphrases her account of aridity in the Life; confirm it isn't overstated. No number of years given.
'The Lord has already pulled up the weeds and put in good plants' follows Life ch. 11; confirm.
Trapdoor third floor: mapping (first water = meditation, second = prayer of quiet, third = sleep of the faculties, fourth = union) simplified; confirm.
Week end (1128–1134): the look-back names Lady Poverty, perfect joy, brother and sister creatures, Make me an instrument, Preach always and Carmel.
No original-language word: Spanish 'agua' felt too thin to teach; original set to null.
